narrative:
The model predicted a 69% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is far below the average of roughly 6 among students who were admitted, signaling that your later-year performance was unusually weak compared with successful applicants.

Your first-year class ranking was the next most important factor and also increased the chance of failure. Again, a decile of 1 is much lower than the average of 6 seen in accepted students.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 3.80 it is noticeably higher than the 3.23 average of admitted students, which helped pull the prediction back toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the two weak class-rank signals.

Your LSAT score of 33 (versus an admitted average of 37), middle-family income, and plan to attend full-time played smaller roles and did not change the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance in law school so that your class rank improves significantly. Retaking the LSAT for a higher score could also help. Once you have stronger evidence of consistent high performance, you should reapply.
